en: Its cannon bone is a handgrip long,
It has the signs of a cripple.
Its heel is a handgrip long;
It has the signs of a nag.
Tossing its forelock, shaking its head,
It shows a skittish nature.
When men joust with pole-like spears,
It shows a nature prone to flight.
A fidgety horse with a slow pacing gait,
If you travel for six months,
This horse will falter and not go on.
If you ride toward Zhet-Kayt,
If you travel seventy days and nights,
It looks unable even to trot.
If there is a white banner and flag,
If there is a shouting tumult,
It shows a nature prone to flight.
It has no courageous mane and tail;
May it not grieve you in combat.
It is no beast to ride into battle.
When your entrusted life is pressed hard,
And all your watching enemies arrive,
When a great host comes gleaming,
When you roar and thrust your spear,
Battle cries deafening the ears,
When you stand face to face,
Even a saddle-shaped ridge,
It is a beast that would fail to cross.
If your precious life were hard pressed,
Your wretched gray horse
Is a beast that would cease to move.
Its ears are long, its body slack;
It is a beast born weak.
Like a pig with a narrow anus,
It has a frail appearance.
If it travels a distant road,
It would pant and cease to move;
It shows that poor character.
A wobbling horse with a slow pacing gait—
Let it go its way; do not covet it.
When you face an enemy you encounter,
Its shoulders and head wobbling,
It is a beast that would fail you.
You yourself upon its back,
Filling you utterly with regret,
It is a beast that would humiliate you.
I shall grant what you ask.
This old man who speaks to you—
If you live, my blue-maned one,
I shall become a father to you!
Understand my words well.
If your lionhood is true,
My lion son, heed my words!
If we ride onward from here,
There is a shrine called Baabedin.
The wise say, and warriors say,
‘It is Father Baabedin's ridge;
Father Adam and Mother Eve
Came together here;
It is the place where they made merry.’
Wondrous things and interesting words—
Let us steep ourselves in wisdom.
Go and see Boz-Talaa.
For a period of six months,
My son Manas, heed my words;
Let us set up a camp together!
Let the horse fatten and become fit;
Before six months are fulfilled,
Let the warrior fatten and become firm!
Let us summer on the face of Ak-Talaa;
Let us sow a good crop of grain!
Let us lay in ample provisions.
Let us open the ground with hoes;
Let us scatter seed by handfuls!
A warrior will come, a lion will come.
Now, Manas, hear my words:
Your wished-for equal will come.
Heed my words, my foal.
Do not take shame, do not feel dishonored;
Let us dwell in Boz-Talaa.
Dividing a black hair exactly in two,
Leopard Manas, hear my words:
Let us sow grain in partnership!
The grain will ripen in six months;
Until that grain ripens,
Let us dwell in Boz-Talaa!”
At those words the old man spoke,
The lion Manas rejoiced:
“Let me dig the earth with a hoe;
Let me eat my fill in plenty!
I swung a spear and broke their ranks;
I made his heart content as ashes spread smooth.
For my ill-intentioned father,
The Kara-Kalmyks and Manzhuu,
I raided them utterly,
Increased his countless herds,
And made him a formidable, swollen rich man.
Where is my father Jakyp's gratitude!
Gathering wealth and keeping livestock,
What inheritance shall I gain?
Better that I should now
Become a grower of grain.
Let me heed the elder's words;
In this Boz-Talaa,
Let me sow a crop in partnership.”
With that old man he had met,
With that being from the unseen,
He made a firm promise,
Spoke words invoking God,
And made a true, firm pledge.
He dwelt in Boz-Talaa;
Your blue-maned hero sowed grain.
From the spur where the mountains ended,
From the plain beyond eyesight,
Before a word or two could be spoken,
In the opening and shutting of an eye,
Taking a shortcut along a narrow path,
That old man brought
Two oxen by their leads.
The yoke-pins were made ready.
That old man he had met
Led the paired oxen.
Khan Manas took hold of the plow;
He opened the face of the earth,
He scattered seed by handfuls.
Sowing grain in partnership,
The blue-maned hero calmed his heart.
The boy heeded the old man's words;
Your bloodthirsty leopard Manas
Put childish ways aside.
His heart filled with wisdom.
The two oxen they had driven there
Vanished from sight.
His father in the open waste,
The old man became his fortress.
He slept, propped on an elbow,
Took a peaceful little doze,
Lay on his side to rest his life,
And lay until his sleep was satisfied.
Starting awake from sleep,
Turning to his right,
He looked toward the elder:
Ruddy wheat filled the place.
The white wheat that remained ready
Had grown to the size of a mountain.
That blessed one, known as a saint,
While Manas slept and rose,
Had made it all ready.
Mighty Manas stood astonished;
Amazed, he turned his head.
“This is a marvel!” he said.
Your blue-maned hero, born fortunate,
Stood utterly astonished.
The old man spoke a word,
Bringing a troubling word to thought:
“O my child Manas, hear my words.
I knew that you were a lion.
When you moved here from Altay,
I had wished to meet you.
I set your crooked course straight.
My valiant one, touched by Khizir,
I became your companion.
We sowed grain in partnership;
Until six months, seven months had passed,
We remained companions.
From now onward, my Manas,
Be a leopard, be a lion.
May your treasures and possessions be complete;
May your hostile enemies be diminished;
May all twelve of your members be whole!
You are my champion, my support,
The lion in whom I place my hope!
A true Muslim of the Islamic faith,
You are my truly worshipping warrior.
I had known news of you.
‘May that dear blue-maned one come,’ I said;
I had yearned for you!
We met and grew gray together,
My valiant one, touched by Khizir;
We became friends until Judgment Day.
We chewed flour of white wheat;
He gave you the name of Lion.
You and I joined together
And sowed a crop in partnership.
We lay close, side by side;
Our lives became united.
I shall take no grain of wheat.
What is seen today is gone tomorrow;
Such is this mischievous world!
On this thieving world,
Even if I die, I shall not set my eyes!
I am a remedy for the people;
I am a thick-armed hero.
To the poor, worn and destitute,
I am especially close.
I am Father Baabedin's eye;
Who feeds all living beings,
I am Baabedin himself.
I sought and knew your lionhood.
By all his rightful earnings, his brow’s sweat,
Let the fortunate one find his horse’—
My child Manas, hear my words—
‘Let the campaigner find his horse,’ I said,
And camped in the open waste.
I dwelt upon this plain.
‘Let the fleet-footed khan find his horse’—
My child Manas, hear my words—
Becoming your friend,
I sowed grain in partnership.
I am the farmer's voice;
Transformed into an old man,
I am Babadyykan himself.
Hearing from the old man of the unseen,
That, escaping a fierce enemy,
My bloodthirsty one was coming, I heard.
Hearing from the earlier old man,
From the unruly Kalmyk enemy,
Fleet-footed Manas, the leopard,
Would escape and come, I heard.
I had come here on purpose.
Come, Manas, my foal,
I knew you lacked a horse!
If the Kakan-chyn people attacked,
‘How will Manas fare?’ I asked,
And went about in sorrow.
Becoming your friend, my champion,
I enticed you into sowing grain.
My reason for enticing you was this:
The peerless steed beneath me—
‘Let him buy and ride it honestly,’ I said;
For that I made provision.
I am Babadyykan.
Take your wheat yourself;
I shall take not one round grain.
My child, attain your heart's desire.
Who feeds all living beings,
I am your father Babadyykan.
Meeting you in the open waste,
I am becoming your friend.
I knew long ago that you would come,
Imposing hero Manas.
‘Let me undo one of his hobbles,’ I said;
That is what I had been asking.
For this wheat that fills the land—
It is also true that you are a lion,
My Manas, may you turn devotedly to God.
You are not Manas for nothing.
My Allah named you Lion
And spread your name throughout the world.
If you ride into battle, Akkula—
That beast is a true peerless steed.
Allah Most High, the one God,
Created him suited to you.
In Beejin of Kakan-chyn,
Six years before your birth,
Your lion's name was inscribed.
